items.title: Security Signal Weekly: November 21-27, 2026
items.content_html:
Overview

This week’s urgent work is concentrated in systems that already have broad authority: collaboration servers tied to Active Directory, virtualization and network control planes, a firewall management interface, an email-security platform, a package registry, and third-party code that runs inside customer websites. Several vendors shipped fixes before defenders learned how much attackers had already done. MiCollab, Xen Orchestra, Juniper Session Smart, Drupal, PAN-OS, and N-able Mail Assure all need some combination of patching and retrospective investigation, not a closed ticket based on a current version alone.

The incident reports carry the same lesson beyond vulnerability management. Hex.pm could verify that packages were not modified but could not rule out database reads. Optimizely removed injected JavaScript, while affected customers still need to understand what ran on their own sites. Reports involving Radware and Cleverbridge move the response into cloud credentials and payment cards, where the useful evidence sits outside the compromised provider.

Reality check: A fixed version proves what is running now. It does not prove an exposed server was clean yesterday, a stolen token was never used, or injected code left no downstream evidence.

Top 10 Security Signals

1. MiCollab zero-days reached identity and backup systems before the patch

What happened: Mitel updated MISA-2026-0012 for five flaws in MiCollab’s Audio, Web and Video Conferencing component, including unauthenticated XML and command injection. Accenture APEX Labs says attackers used the flaws before Mitel’s November 16 advisory, reached root on one MiCollab server within 30 minutes, moved into identity infrastructure, and later accessed backup and database systems. CISA added all five CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 25. Accenture assesses that AI-assisted tooling probably supported part of the activity, but its sampled telemetry cannot show exactly how the services were used.

Why it matters: MiCollab is not an isolated phone server when it holds directory credentials and can reach internal services. A team that installed the patch after November 16 may have closed the entry point while leaving web shells, stolen credentials, altered logs, or activity on downstream systems untouched.

Action:

  • Apply Mitel’s patch for release 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or move to a later fixed release, then verify the running build and patch state on every MiCollab node.
  • Use Accenture’s indicators and host artifacts to examine MiCollab systems from before November 16, including outbound connections, web-shell locations, local-log gaps, and unexpected privileged commands.
  • If compromise is possible, rotate the directory and service credentials available to MiCollab and review domain controllers, backup servers, and database systems the appliance could reach.

2. Xen Orchestra authentication bypass became a hypervisor takeover path

What happened: Vates says CVE-2026-133469 lets an unauthenticated request present an empty JSON object as an authentication token and obtain an existing user’s access. The Vates advisory documents active exploitation, malicious virtual-machine changes, and persistence on XCP-ng hosts. Versions 6.9.2 and 6.10.1 contain the fix, and CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 25.

Why it matters: Xen Orchestra can control virtual machines, hypervisor hosts, backups, and the credentials used to connect them. Administrative access to that plane can become root-level persistence below the guest operating systems, where rebuilding only the management appliance would leave the attacker in place.

Action:

  • Update Xen Orchestra to 6.9.2 on the stable channel or 6.10.1 on the latest channel, and update xo-server to the fixed package for the selected channel.
  • Remove Xen Orchestra from direct internet reach and limit it to a dedicated management network; use Vates’ published network and host indicators to check the appliance and every managed pool.
  • If compromise is confirmed, follow Vates’ clean-reinstallation guidance for affected management and hypervisor systems and rotate pool, backup, directory, mail, proxy, user, and OTP secrets.

3. Juniper Session Smart Conductor flaw gives unauthenticated attackers root

What happened: Juniper updated its Session Smart security bulletin on November 24 after receiving a report of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406. A crafted Salt minion identifier can reach the Conductor’s AutomatedProvisioner and execute commands as root without authentication. Fixed releases are 7.0.5, 7.1.7, and 7.2.3, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the next day.

Why it matters: The Conductor manages the routers in its authority, so root access is a control-plane incident rather than one compromised Linux host. Juniper lists no workaround, and router-to-Conductor communication can make the service reachable across network boundaries that an ordinary management portal would not cross.

Action:

  • Upgrade each Session Smart Conductor to 7.0.5, 7.1.7, 7.2.3, or a later fixed release and verify the version after every node returns to service.
  • Restrict Conductor ports and administrative access to the exact routers and management sources that require them instead of allowing broad untrusted reachability.
  • Preserve Conductor logs and inspect root-level commands, Salt key activity, configuration changes, new accounts, persistence, and changes pushed to managed routers during the exposed period.

4. Drupal confirms its installer flaw was exploited on live sites

What happened: Drupal’s SA-CORE-2026-017 advisory says attackers can use install.php under specific conditions to attempt a reinstall, leading to site takeover or remote code execution. The security team received a report of exploitation on live sites as early as November 19. The fixed branches begin at Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, and 11.4.13, and CISA added CVE-2026-132165 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 24.

Why it matters: A successful reinstall can change the site, its database connection, and administrative control in one sequence. Some server permissions reduce the attack paths, but Drupal explicitly says they do not mitigate every path, so a hardened settings.php is not a substitute for the security release.

Action:

  • Update to the fixed release for the site’s supported Drupal branch and verify the deployed code and container or host actually use it.
  • Follow Drupal’s installer-hardening guidance, including web-server restrictions around install.php and permissions that prevent settings.php from being rewritten.
  • Review web, PHP, file-integrity, database, and administrator activity from November 19 onward; rebuild from a trusted source and rotate application secrets when takeover evidence appears.

5. Attackers are chaining PHP2Shell with a PAN-OS kernel flaw

What happened: The October 23 edition covered PHP2Shell when attackers were probing the PHP flaws before patches arrived. The new development is a confirmed appliance attack chain. Palo Alto Networks says CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel privilege-escalation flaw fixed across supported PAN-OS branches, has been exploited against management interfaces exposed to the internet. The observed path first uses PHP2Shell to reach the interface and then CVE-2026-46300 to raise privileges.

Why it matters: Updating PHP closes the first step, but it does not answer whether an attacker already gained a shell or root access on the firewall. A compromised management plane can expose configuration, credentials, and policy while sitting in the path defenders depend on to contain other systems.

Action:

  • Match every PAN-OS device to the fixed versions in the advisory, update both the PHP2Shell and kernel components through the supported PAN-OS release, and verify each high-availability peer.
  • Remove management profiles from internet-facing dataplane interfaces and allow administrative access only from named internal or out-of-band sources.
  • For any device whose management interface was publicly reachable, investigate the pre-patch window for PHP2Shell requests, process execution, configuration changes, new accounts, exported data, and persistence before returning it to trust.

6. The Hex package registry contained remote code execution but cannot rule out database reads

What happened: On November 23, an attacker sent 69 exploit requests that ran commands on six registry web servers. The Hex incident report says the team blocked the traffic and replaced the servers with a patched build within about 20 minutes. Hex found no unexpected package changes or database writes, but database reads were not logged, so it cannot rule out access to email addresses, password hashes, two-factor secrets, sessions, audit logs, or some private package data. The project rotated infrastructure credentials and session keys and assigned CVE-2026-129514.

Why it matters: The absence of modified packages narrows the software-supply-chain risk, but it does not make account exposure disappear. Package registries connect developer identities, organization memberships, private code, and publishing authority, so a stolen session or 2FA secret can outlive the short server intrusion.

Action:

  • Change the Hex account password, reset the authenticator-app setup to issue a new two-factor secret and recovery codes, and review organization membership and audit activity.
  • Update Hex clients when the new rotatable registry-signing system is released; until then, fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm and not third-party mirrors.
  • Treat unexpected Hex-themed email as likely follow-on phishing, verify links independently, and revoke or rotate publishing credentials when account activity cannot be explained.

7. N-able Mail Assure incident puts an email-security control on the response list

What happened: N-able says it remediated CVE-2026-134624 and restored the Mail Assure dashboard and APIs on November 21. The vendor’s incident update says it found no exploitation beyond one N-able-hosted server and engaged an outside forensics team. The flaw affects Mail Assure and SpamExperts builds before 20261121.1943 and lets an authenticated API user make the service connect to internal hosts through the LDAP synchronization check. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 23.

Why it matters: Email-security platforms are trusted by MSPs to sit in the mail path and integrate with customer environments. A server-side request forgery path can turn that trusted service into a way to probe or reach internal systems, while a cloud-hosted fix still leaves customers responsible for checking the access and credentials on their side of the integration.

Action:

  • Confirm every self-hosted or partner-managed Mail Assure and SpamExperts environment is on build 20261121.1943 or later; for N-able-hosted service, retain the vendor notice and identify which tenants and integrations were in scope.
  • Review Mail Assure API users, relay and LDAP synchronization settings, administrative changes, and connections to internal addresses during the incident window.
  • Rotate suspicious API or integration credentials and follow N-able’s forthcoming root-cause analysis for any additional tenant-specific checks rather than assuming restored mail flow closes the incident.

8. Optimizely account impersonation pushed malicious JavaScript into customer sites

What happened: Optimizely says an attacker exploited its Web Experimentation account-signup flow on November 16, impersonated users on targeted customer accounts, and inserted malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The vendor advisory says fewer than 5% of customers were affected, delivery was blocked within three hours of detection, and the injected code was removed. CISA added CVE-2026-132224 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 24.

Why it matters: Experimentation snippets are designed to execute code in a customer’s site and can reach visitors across many pages. Removing the injected project code stops future delivery, but the affected organization is the one with the web, checkout, content-security-policy, and client-side telemetry needed to determine what visitors received before containment.

Action:

  • Confirm directly with Optimizely whether each Web Experimentation account was affected and preserve the vendor notice, project history, user activity, and the exact containment times.
  • Compare published project JavaScript and snippet changes with approved releases, then review browser-security, web, checkout, and fraud telemetry for the affected delivery window.
  • Remove stale users, enforce strong authentication, tighten who can publish project code, and require a review path for changes that execute across production pages.

9. Radware customers may need to rotate cloud log-export credentials

What happened: BleepingComputer reports that an internal Radware root-cause report describes an unauthenticated Cloud WAF management API exposed to the internet and accessed on November 19. The potentially accessed information includes customer contact data and, for a subset of customers, AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or SFTP credentials configured for log export. Radware had not published a public statement when the report appeared, so the affected-customer count and evidence of downstream credential use remain unsettled.

Why it matters: A WAF provider does not need access to an application database for this incident to spread. Log-export keys can lead into customer-controlled storage that contains security telemetry, request details, and operational context, and an attempted login may appear only in the customer’s cloud audit trail.

Action:

  • If Radware notifies the organization, rotate every Cloud WAF log-export key, SAS token, or SFTP credential named in the notice and invalidate the old value.
  • Review AWS, Azure, and SFTP access records from at least November 19 for unfamiliar source addresses, object reads, listings, permission changes, or failed attempts using the old credential.
  • Replace broad account keys with a dedicated least-privilege identity limited to the required log destination, and record what data the exporter could read or write while the old credential was valid.

10. Cleverbridge breach notifications include card numbers and security codes

What happened: Cleverbridge detected unauthorized activity on November 4 and began notifying affected buyers on November 20. According to BleepingComputer’s reporting and a notification it reviewed, the copied data for affected people includes payment-card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV or CVC security codes. Cleverbridge has not disclosed how the attacker entered, how many people were affected, or which software merchants’ customers are represented.

Why it matters: Cleverbridge processes purchases and subscriptions for many software companies, so a buyer may recognize the software brand but not the payment provider named in the notice. Card data with the security code creates an immediate fraud concern, while the incomplete public scope gives criminals room to send convincing fake refund, replacement-card, or account-warning messages.

Action:

  • Affected cardholders should contact the card issuer through a trusted number, follow its replacement guidance, and monitor transactions and alerts instead of replying to the breach email with payment details.
  • Software vendors that use Cleverbridge should confirm whether their buyers are in scope, prepare a support response with the official notification path, and warn that neither vendor will request a full card number or security code by email, text, or phone.
  • Preserve the notice and transaction details for dispute or incident records, and keep the unknown victim count, entry method, and dwell time marked as unknown until Cleverbridge publishes more evidence.

Closing Notes

Start with MiCollab, Xen Orchestra, Juniper Session Smart, Drupal, and internet-exposed PAN-OS management because exploitation is confirmed and several paths end in root or administrative control. Put an owner beside the retrospective checks as well as the updates. Hex and N-able require account and integration review even though the providers contained their known server activity.

For Optimizely, Radware, and Cleverbridge, the useful evidence belongs partly to customers: browser and checkout telemetry, cloud-storage audit logs, and card activity. Provider remediation changes what can happen next. It does not replace the customer’s work to establish what happened before containment.

items.title: When the Security Agent Goes Quiet, Your Dashboard Needs an Exception
items.content_html:
A quiet endpoint is not necessarily a healthy endpoint. If its security agent has stopped reporting, an empty alert list leaves a question open: what can we actually see?

I want a coverage report to make that question easy to answer. A green percentage is useful only when I can account for the devices behind it, including the ones that have gone quiet. For an MSP, that means reconciling the security console with the asset list and giving every unresolved gap an owner.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint provides a useful example of how to approach this. The workflow below is general practitioner guidance, not a real-client investigation. The aim is to turn an unexplained inventory row into a documented decision.

Read the health state before choosing the fix

Defender separates Sensor health state from Onboarding status. A device appearing in the inventory is not, by itself, proof that its sensor is reporting. Microsoft’s device inventory field reference lists Active, Inactive, and Misconfigured, with Impaired communications and No sensor data under Misconfigured in the portal filter.

I would use those labels to choose the next question:

Reported stateWhat I would check next
ActiveDoes the recent signal belong to the expected device identity?
InactiveIs the asset still in service, and when should it next be online?
Impaired communicationsCan the sensor reach the service through its required network path?
No sensor dataWhat telemetry is missing, and what communication still works?
Not onboardedIs this an asset we are responsible for protecting, and has onboarding been assigned?

The last row is an onboarding question, not another sensor-health value. Keeping those fields separate prevents a discovered device from being counted as a functioning EDR deployment.

Microsoft’s sensor-health guidance describes inactive devices as having stopped reporting for more than seven days in the past month. That is a product reporting threshold. I would set the team’s investigation timing around the device’s importance and expected use, rather than waiting a week to notice a production system has gone silent.

Reconcile the asset and its identity

Start with the list of devices the organization expects to manage. Establish who owns the asset, whether it is still in service, and whether it should be online. Then compare that expectation with the RMM, security inventory, and onboarding or retirement records.

A hostname is a useful search term. I would also compare the device identifiers and available asset records before deciding that two rows represent the same machine, or that one missing row proves a device is gone.

Microsoft’s unhealthy-sensor guidance describes unused, reinstalled, renamed, and offboarded devices as reasons for inactive records. It also explains that an old inactive entity can remain after a reinstall or rename while a new entity reports normally.

That changes the next action. A retired laptop needs verified retirement records. A rebuilt machine needs its current identity reconciled with the old one. An active workstation with no current signal needs investigation. Reinstalling the agent before answering those questions can leave the inventory problem unresolved.

Check what the timestamp actually measures

Record the last trustworthy signal, its source, and its time zone. An RMM check-in tells me when the RMM heard from the device. It does not establish when the EDR service last received useful telemetry.

There is also a distinction within Defender. Microsoft says Last device update in the inventory reflects its refresh cadence, typically up to daily, and can lag behind fresher last-seen information on the device page or in Advanced hunting. The field reference explains that timestamp.

I would inspect the device detail before declaring a repair unsuccessful because a summary row still looks stale. Equally, I would not close the work from a current timestamp without checking which record and signal it represents.

Work from reachability toward sensor health

For a device that should be active, confirm that it is powered on and reachable through a trusted management path. Check that the expected security component is present and running, then investigate the service’s connectivity and relevant configuration.

On Windows, Defender’s EDR sensor runs as LocalSystem and uses WinHTTP. Its proxy configuration is independent of WinINet settings, and the EDR sensor and Microsoft Defender Antivirus have separate proxy settings. Microsoft’s Windows proxy guidance explains those distinctions.

My practical conclusion is that a working browser or remote-support session is only one piece of evidence. Test the sensor’s required path using the vendor’s troubleshooting guidance for the actual platform and deployment.

No sensor data does not settle the connectivity question

Microsoft’s unhealthy-sensor troubleshooting page describes this state as possible even when the device communicates with the service and reports partial data. Investigate the missing telemetry and the communication that remains; the label alone is not proof of a complete network outage.

Response capability deserves attention too. Microsoft notes that impaired communications can prevent actions such as isolation, file blocking, or sending files for analysis. If a response is needed, verify its actual result and follow the incident process when the action cannot be confirmed.

Give every visibility exception an owner

The report I want alongside a coverage percentage is a short list of unresolved devices, what is known about each one, and who is doing what next. Here, an exception means a tracked gap in visibility. It is not an antivirus exclusion or permission to disable a control.

A hypothetical report might cover 100 assets expected to have EDR, with 97 meeting the team’s current reporting criterion. The other three still need to appear: perhaps one is awaiting an approved retirement check, one is intentionally offline, and one has an unexplained sensor problem. Those are different decisions, even if the dashboard gives all three the same status.

Define the reporting criterion and the expected population alongside the percentage. Remove a retired asset from that population only after its retirement is verified. Keep intentionally offline devices visible with a return date or review point instead of treating silence as success.

An exception record to copy into your ticket

Replace these prompts with actual findings. This is a working template, not a completed investigation.

  • Asset and identity: Expected asset, owner, current device ID, and any previous identity being reconciled.
  • Expected state: In service, intentionally offline, pending retirement, or another documented state.
  • Observed state: Sensor health, onboarding status, and the source and time of the observation.
  • Last reliable signal: Telemetry source, timestamp, time zone, and any freshness limit.
  • Investigation: Checks performed, evidence, likely cause, and what remains unknown.
  • Next action: Named owner, action, due date, and escalation point if visibility cannot be restored.
  • Resolution evidence: Fresh telemetry from the correct device, verified retirement, or an explicitly approved temporary disposition with a review date.

Keep the device identifiers and supporting evidence in the private service record. A client-facing summary can explain the remaining work without reproducing sensitive inventory details.

Close the loop with evidence of recovery

An installation script returning success is a useful step. Before closing the ticket, I would confirm that the correct device identity is present, that fresh telemetry has arrived, and that the observed sensor health matches the intended result. Record when and where those checks were made.

Restored reporting establishes visibility going forward. It does not, by itself, explain what happened during the gap. If that gap matters to an ongoing investigation, preserve its start and end points and document the limits of the available evidence. This is the same principle behind my endpoint quarantine investigation checklist: the closeout should say what was verified and what still needs attention.

If a laptop is intentionally offline until its owner returns, keep that disposition explicit and assign the follow-up. Unknown is a useful status when it leads to a next action. A dashboard becomes more credible when the missing devices remain part of the conversation.

For your own endpoint reviews, what is the first field you check when an agent stops reporting? I would start with the last trustworthy check-in, then reconcile whether the asset is still supposed to be active.

items.title: Black Friday Prep and a Good Kind of Busy (Week 47, 2026)
items.content_html:
The vibe

Feeling pretty great and accomplished. It has been a busy week, but the good kind of busy. I have had plenty to keep me occupied, and it feels good to see things coming together.

Highlights

  • 🛍️ I got Trayage’s Black Friday offer out. There is a 30% discount on the one-time cleanup unlock, and I put the details and redemption links together on the site. I am still figuring out the marketing side of this whole indie-dev thing. LOL.

  • ✉️ A little RelayByte housekeeping. I worked on email signatures for my personal and support emails. Small thing, but I wanted them to look like they belonged to the studio. Even the boring bits need some attention.

  • ✍️ I made some time for writing, too. There was some drafting and revising in the mix. Not everything is ready to put out yet, but it felt good to get some of it into better shape.

Worth sharing

  • How do you share a good read? I asked this on Mastodon while sharing Drift. I built it so I could start with the passage that caught my attention, then add my own thoughts before sharing. Curious whether other people prefer that or just posting the link.
  • Google’s COLD RELIC case study was one of the security reads I shared. The part that caught my attention was the attacker keeping access through passkeys that survived password and session resets. Worth a read if you look after Google Workspace.

✌️ That is it for this week. I hope you have a great week and remember to be kind to each other!

items.title: An Outlook Spoofing Advisory Isn't a Complete Incident Story
items.content_html:
If someone calls the help desk and says they opened a suspicious email in Outlook, my first question would be, “Did you read the email, or did you open a file attached to it?” For CVE-2026-124194, that detail changes what I’d investigate. Microsoft says the flaw requires someone to open a specially prepared file in an affected copy of Outlook. It explicitly rules out the Preview Pane.

Microsoft rated the flaw Moderate when it published the advisory on November 10. It also reported that attackers had exploited it. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog that same day. For an MSP deciding which November updates to chase on overdue laptops, I’d give the observed exploitation more weight than the severity label. Telling a client that one of their users was affected takes evidence from that client.

What the missing Outlook warning can expose

The word spoofing might send a technician looking at the From address. Microsoft’s description points to something the sender field can’t show. When Outlook opens the file, it can contact an external system without giving the user its usual warning. In doing so, it can disclose NTLMv2 authentication data that an attacker could use to impersonate the user. Microsoft classifies the weakness as CWE-356, an inadequate warning about an unsafe action. The advisory’s FAQ explains both the interaction and the potential disclosure.

That changes the conversation with the person who reported the message. “I didn’t type my password” is entirely consistent with the risk Microsoft describes. Ask which file they opened, on which device, and roughly when. If they only viewed the message in the reading pane, record that answer. They can report the original through the usual phishing-reporting channel without reopening the file to show the help desk what it did.

Match the fix to the copy of Office on the device

Microsoft’s November advisory lists 32-bit and 64-bit editions of Office LTSC 2021, Office LTSC 2024, and Microsoft 365 Apps for enterprise. That’s a desktop software inventory question. A list of Exchange Online mailboxes won’t tell you which build of Outlook the person used.

These are the November 10 fixes in Microsoft’s product and remediation data and its Office security release notes. Use the row for the installed product and servicing channel when checking a later release.

Installed productNovember 10 fix
Office LTSC 2021Build 16.0.14334.21048
Office LTSC 2024Build 16.0.17932.21140
Microsoft 365 Apps for enterpriseVaries by channel and version. For version 2610, Current Channel received 20527.20196 and Monthly Enterprise Channel received 20527.20194.

A fleet report that treats 20527.20196 as the minimum for every device on version 2610 would put an already-patched Monthly Enterprise laptop back in the queue. Microsoft’s build history by channel also lists the November releases for devices on versions 2609 and 2608. Compare each device with its own branch.

In classic Outlook on Windows, File → Office Account shows the product version and build. I’d put that observation, or a fresh device inventory showing the same information, in the patch ticket. Include when it was collected. If a laptop last checked in before the update went out, give someone ownership of checking it when it returns. Counting the deployment as a success today can take that laptop off tomorrow’s work list.

What to put in the incident ticket

Suppose someone in accounts payable reports that a supplier sent new bank details in an attachment. Accounts payable can hold the change and call the supplier using the number already on file. They don’t need to wait for IT to finish examining the message before protecting the payment.

On the technical side, preserve the original message and headers. Use the message ID in Exchange Online message trace to establish who received it and when. A delivery timestamp gives the investigation a starting point. Whether somebody opened the attached file is a question for the recipient and the endpoint records.

If the recipient opened the file, check which Outlook build was running at the time. Use endpoint or proxy records to see whether Outlook contacted an unfamiliar destination around the reported opening time. If the connection looks related, preserve the records and escalate the possible credential exposure through the client’s incident process. Include the account and time window so the responder can check subsequent authentication activity.

The awkward case is the laptop that updated overnight. By morning, the technician can verify the fix and accounts payable can confirm the payment was held. The question still open is which build handled the file yesterday afternoon. I’d put that question in the handoff, along with who’s checking the device’s update history. Otherwise the next person to pick up the ticket sees a current build and has every reason to think the work is done.

items.title: Duo Fun, Client Work, and a Dispatch Goodbye (Weeks 45 & 46, 2026)
items.content_html:
I missed last week’s notes, so I am combining Weeks 45 and 46 into one post. These cover November 2 through November 15.

The vibe

A mix of fun and frustration. I am still having a great time with the iPhone Duo and working on new ideas, but my health has had its ups and downs. That is always a battle, and I am trying to stay strong through it.

Highlights

  • 📱 I am still having hella fun with the iPhone Duo. This phone is amazing. The more I use it, the less sure I am that I could ever go back to a slab phone again.

  • 💬 I decided to go back to X/Twitter. I have been posting more there lately and getting way more engagement there and on Mastodon.

  • 🔎 Work has included tracking down phishing attempts at client sites. A few involved PDFs in emails, so I have been digging into those. I have also been setting up Conditional Access rules for a client after our SaaS Alerts monitoring picked up sign-in alerts from different countries. Those alerts were a reason to take a closer look at the client’s sign-in controls.

  • 🏠 I am still on the work-from-home wagon. Not complaining, though.

  • 💻 The solo founder work continues. I am still trying to get the first sale of my Mac app. I am by no means a marketer. LOL. I have also been working on a few app and SaaS ideas, so there is plenty to keep me busy on that front.

Week 45

  • ✍️ There was a lot of writing. I published reviews of TypeDraw Notebook, Showcase, MoneyCoach, Lume, and Cassette Player. I also wrote about an LXD MicroCloud certificate bypass and put together a Conditional Access rollout checklist for MSPs.

  • 📰 Security Signal Weekly was back on Friday. The October 31–November 6 edition rounded up the week’s security news for defenders and MSPs.

Week 46

  • 📬 I ended The Defender’s Dispatch after 13 issues. Putting together both the web edition and the email every week had become stressful, and I did not want to keep promising a schedule that was wearing on me. I am glad I made it, and I appreciate everyone who read, subscribed, or sent a story. Issue 013 was the last one; the archive will stay online. I wrote a short note about the decision, too. I will keep writing here, including Security Signal Weekly.

  • 🔒 I wrote about what comes after a security alert or a patch. The SonicWall SSL VPN article looks at the authentication paths MSPs need to check after patching the SAML bypass. Later in the week, I wrote a quarantine investigation checklist for working through what a security product actually contained, how a file arrived, and what still needs checking before a ticket closes.

  • ☁️ The Microsoft 365 outage became another article. I looked at the November 12–13 outage and its impact on businesses and schools, including what IT teams and MSPs can do when the service they rely on for customer communication is having trouble itself.

  • ⭐ I added a Tech Review badge to the site. Articles tagged as reviews now show the badge in listings and on the article itself, making those posts easier to spot.

✌️ That is it for these past two weeks. I hope you have a great week and remember to be kind to each other!

items.title: Microsoft 365’s Global Outage: What Happened and What It Means for IT
items.content_html:
When email stops working, the first question is usually whether something is wrong with the computer. When calendars, customer communications, and parts of the support process start failing together, that question gets much bigger.

The Microsoft 365 outage that began on Thursday, November 12, and continued into Friday, November 13, is a reminder of how much everyday work depends on the same underlying services. A business might describe Microsoft as its email provider. Its actual dependency can extend into scheduling, document workflows, security administration, and the tools other vendors have built around its data.

I’m looking at this from the IT and managed service provider side: what Microsoft has established, what affected organizations are reporting, and what we should be able to do when the repair is outside our control.

Status at the time of writing

This account was checked on November 13, 2026, at 9:57 a.m. Central Standard Time (15:57 UTC). Microsoft’s 14:56 UTC public service-health update reported sustained improvements in service availability, with intermittent connectivity problems and delayed email still possible. Microsoft was validating recovery and addressing remaining issues. Full mitigation remained pending. Microsoft said it had no evidence of malicious activity and would publish a post-incident report.

November 26 update: Microsoft’s final incident report

When I first wrote this, the cause was still open. Microsoft’s November 20 post-incident report for EX1550543 and MO1550821 traces the outage to a Windows defect in the configuration used by Exchange Online’s gateways. Maintenance had reduced available capacity, Teams traffic had shifted onto those gateways, and peak demand exposed the defect. Load tests hadn’t reproduced that traffic mix on the newer hardware. As servers stopped responding, automatic rerouting sent more traffic to gateways with the same defect, first in North America and then in other regions.

Microsoft says active customer impact ended at 10:10 a.m. CST on November 13. It declared the incident resolved at 10:15 p.m. CST that evening after monitoring recovery and clearing the backlog. Queued enterprise mail was delivered. Some delayed messages to inactive consumer mailboxes expired.

Microsoft lists narrower regional failover and separate gateway pools for different workloads as follow-up work. Here’s the test I’d run at an MSP: if email is down, can a customer still get an urgent ticket to a technician without going through the same mailbox, sign-in, or integration?

What happened, and what is still unknown

Microsoft’s incident record gives Exchange Online incident EX1550543 a start time of 16:17 UTC on November 12, or 10:17 a.m. CST. The broader Microsoft 365 incident, MO1550821, followed at 18:26 UTC, or 12:26 p.m. CST. These are the vendor’s recorded incident times, not a claim that every customer lost service simultaneously. The University of Pennsylvania publishes a public extract of Microsoft’s incident messages.

Those updates described servers becoming unavailable and transferring load to the remaining infrastructure. Microsoft later identified an overwhelmed process responsible for secure connections. Recovery involved traffic changes, restarts, and configuration work; some early changes did not take effect as expected. On Friday morning, Microsoft reported improved stability after a patch to an upstream authentication/routing configuration component. The final root cause was still pending in the Microsoft incident record.

That is enough to explain the operational failure without pretending we have the completed engineering investigation. I want the eventual report to explain the initiating fault, why the failure spread, and which safeguards failed to contain it. A recovery action alone does not answer all three questions.

It also matters that the symptoms varied. Microsoft’s current service breakdown distinguishes affected Exchange-dependent features from functions that remain available:

AreaReported impact or limit
Outlook and Exchange OnlineMailbox access failures and delayed delivery.
TeamsCalendar and other dependent features affected; most core calls, meetings, and chats functioning.
SharePointSome sharing and dependent features affected; direct file access functioning.
Education and CopilotSome learning features and Copilot experiences affected.
Administration and securitySome admin, Defender, and Purview functions degraded.

For a service desk, that detail changes the advice. An existing chat may work while a calendar workflow fails. An affected feature in a product does not tell us the condition of every feature, every tenant, or every device. Check the task the person needs to complete.

The effects reach well beyond an inbox

The strongest examples come from organizations explaining their own disruption. They show how a cloud incident becomes a business or public-service problem.

Companies and their customers

Workhorse Group postponed its third-quarter earnings release and conference call, moving the call from November 12 to November 16 and attributing the change to business disruption from the Microsoft outage. That is a concrete missed business event, not just a count of people refreshing Outlook.

Customer-support platform Pylon reported delayed and failed processing of Outlook and Teams events. It said its engineers had deployed mitigations and planned to backfill missed Outlook email and calendar events after Microsoft recovered.

That second example is especially relevant to IT companies. A customer may submit a request through email and assume it is in the support queue. If the integration has stalled, the team needs another way to receive urgent work and a way to reconcile what arrived late. The health of the ticketing application alone cannot answer whether its email intake is current.

Schools, colleges, and universities

UC Davis told its community that email delivery to both its Microsoft and Google email services was affected. Its notice specifically warned that Outlook and DavisMail users could not reliably send or receive email. That is an important example of local dependencies: having a second vendor in the environment does not automatically make an entire communication path independent.

At Box Hill Institute in Australia, a Friday notice asked students whose weekend assessments were affected to discuss their options with teachers on Monday.

For schools, I would treat communication and deadline decisions as part of the response. Staff need a clear method for receiving urgent parent messages. Students need to know how to report access problems and whether an alternative submission route is available. Teachers should not have to invent a different policy for each class while IT is still establishing what works. Those are continuity decisions for school leadership and IT to make together.

Government and public services

Western Australia’s Training Accreditation Council reported that it could not access Outlook email or receive incoming Teams calls, and directed urgent contacts to LinkedIn. The Shire of Carnarvon published a customer-service mobile number because email was affected and its phone system could also experience disruption.

The Australian Bureau of Meteorology’s notice drew a useful boundary: email contact could be affected, while forecasts and warnings remained available through its website and weather app.

That is the kind of public update I want to see. Explain what people can still do, which channel to use, and what might take longer. Broad statements that an organization is “down” can obscure the services people can still rely on.

What IT companies and MSPs are dealing with

An MSP has two problems to manage at once. Its customers need help, and its own staff may depend on the same email, calendar, and collaboration services.

Maintech’s published account of its service-desk response offers one concrete example. The provider reported a surge in calls and described helping customers with workarounds, communicating through channels outside email, and translating Microsoft’s status updates into practical guidance. This is Maintech’s account of its own response, rather than independent evidence of how every MSP performed.

The difficult part is that the team receiving the calls cannot restart Microsoft’s infrastructure. It still owns the customer relationship, the quality of its advice, and the work that can continue locally.

I would organize that work around four priorities.

Establish scope without creating extra repair work

Check the tenant’s service-health record, compare the reported symptoms, and determine whether unrelated services are also failing. Microsoft documents Health > Service health in the admin center, with the public status page as an alternative when admin access is unavailable.

Once the symptoms match an upstream incident, repeated profile rebuilds, password resets, and reinstallations need a specific justification. I would preserve working sessions and cached data, and keep a separate path for problems that do not fit the vendor incident. A widespread outage should reduce duplicate troubleshooting without becoming an excuse to dismiss every new fault.

Give customers an update they can act on

Use a shared incident record for the common problem and retain each customer’s actual impact. Set an update cadence, name the approved contact channel, and separate a promised update time from an estimated restoration time.

The customer needs to know whether to phone a supplier, postpone a meeting, or use another approved process. Repeating the vendor’s engineering language without translating its practical meaning leaves that decision with the person least equipped to make it.

A customer update structure I would use

This is a template to adapt to verified conditions, not an update sent to any customer.

“Microsoft is investigating incident [ID]. We have confirmed [specific symptoms] in your environment. [Named functions] are still working in our checks. For urgent requests, use [approved channel]. Please report any different symptoms through that channel. Our next update will be at [time and time zone], even if Microsoft has not provided a restoration estimate.”

Keep essential work moving safely

Choose workarounds based on the actual dependency. Moving from desktop Outlook to a browser is useful only if that access method works. Moving to another application that needs the same unavailable mailbox data may leave the workflow just as blocked.

Microsoft’s offline Outlook guidance describes access to locally saved information, subject to the client and its settings. Previously cached mail can help someone find information. It does not establish that a new message has reached its recipient.

I would also make the data-handling boundary explicit. A fallback should be approved for the information involved. An outage is a poor moment to start copying client records, student information, or internal documents into personal accounts with no agreed controls.

Plan the recovery work before the dashboard turns green

A user opening Outlook again is a useful check. It is only one part of recovery.

Test inbound and outbound mail with an external recipient, review failed or delayed messages, and check calendars and connected applications. Reconcile urgent requests that arrived through temporary channels. Pylon’s planned backfill is a good reminder that downstream systems may have their own recovery work after the underlying service returns.

For an MSP, I would record those results per customer. One tenant passing a test should not close every customer’s ticket. Keep the disruption window, observed impact, and remaining actions available for the customer’s own review.

Security teams have a recovery job too

The security implications deserve attention even without evidence of an attack. Microsoft listed degradation affecting parts of Defender and Purview, including access and some policy-related functions. That does not establish that every endpoint stopped protecting itself. It does mean security teams need to check their actual visibility and workflows.

My response would be to record which consoles and actions were available during the incident, preserve independently collected logs, and review delayed alerts or unfinished investigations afterward. I would also remind staff to verify unexpected support requests through a known channel. Someone offering a quick fix during an outage should face the same identity checks as any other unsolicited caller.

Keep temporary exceptions narrow and documented. The need to complete a task does not, by itself, justify removing a protection or granting a new person access.

The larger issue is shared dependency

Microsoft 365 brings a great deal together. That integration is useful: fewer separate systems to administer, connected information, and familiar tools for users. The same connections can also make one service failure interrupt several business processes at once.

I would review resilience at the workflow level. Can the help desk receive an urgent request if email is unavailable? Can the incident lead reach customer contacts without opening the affected directory or mailbox? Can staff find the continuity plan if its usual location is inaccessible? Does the alternative tool require the same sign-in service or data connector?

Those questions are more useful than counting how many vendors appear on a purchasing spreadsheet. UC Davis’s cross-platform mail warning and Pylon’s integration incident both show why the entire path matters.

For the business review, I would also count more than outage duration: staff time diverted, delayed orders or approvals, extra support labor, and the work of reconciling what happened. Each organization needs its own evidence for those costs. Restoring access does not automatically clear the operational backlog.

Buying a second platform also brings cost, administration, training, and data-governance work. I would start with the organization’s most time-sensitive processes, decide how long each can wait, and test a fallback that is proportionate to that need. A reachable phone tree and an accessible contact list may solve an urgent communication problem more effectively than an untested second software subscription.

Backups belong in this discussion, with a clear purpose. In planning terms, recovering a copy of information and keeping a live service available are different requirements. Ask how staff would access the recovered data, how current it would be, and what they could actually do with it during an outage. A restore demonstration should answer those questions.

The eventual Microsoft post-incident report should inform those decisions. I would look for an explanation of the failure’s reach, the difficulty of restoring capacity, and changes that can be tested. Customers should also examine their own response: where updates failed to reach people, which dependencies surprised them, and how much manual work remains.

What I would take into the next outage

For IT teams and MSPs, the practical lesson is to make continuity something people can use under pressure. Know the critical workflows. Keep an approved communication route available outside the affected service. Give staff specific instructions. Verify recovery against the work customers need to complete.

Microsoft owns the repair of its service. The organizations that depend on it still need a plan for the hours in between, and for the unfinished work waiting afterward. That is the part I would want ready before the next incident.

items.title: Quarantine Is a Starting Point, Not a Closed Security Ticket
items.content_html:
An antivirus console says a file was quarantined. The endpoint is online. The user has not called the help desk. That can feel like an easy ticket to close.

I want the ticket to explain more than the last action the security product reported. What arrived, what happened before detection, and what still needs attention are separate questions. A quarantine notification gives me a response claim to verify. It does not supply the whole investigation.

That distinction matters in an MSP, where the antivirus console, EDR platform, RMM, and service desk may each show a different part of the same event. The aim is a proportionate investigation with enough evidence for another analyst to understand the decision.

Start by recording exactly what the tool did

Capture the alert time and time zone, affected endpoint, threat name, file path or object identifier, hash if available, detection engine, relevant policy, and reported action. Keep endpoint identities and other sensitive details in the private investigation record. Preserve a reference to the original alert so the next analyst can find the evidence.

Then verify the result for the affected device. Was an action requested, awaiting approval, still running, successful, or unsuccessful? A submitted command is not a completed response. Record failures and pending work rather than assuming a retry succeeded.

The following distinctions are useful questions to apply to a product’s labels. They are not a universal status dictionary:

Reported stateWhat I would verify next
DetectedWhat was observed, and did the product take a response action?
QuarantinedWhich object and device were affected, and did the action succeed?
Execution blockedWhich execution attempt was prevented, and what happened before it?
Deleted or remediatedWhich artifacts or behaviors did the action address?
Pending or failedWhat remains incomplete, and who owns the next step?

For example, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint’s Stop and quarantine action can stop processes, quarantine files, and remove persistent data. Its results include success, failure, and pending states. I would read those action details before summarizing what was contained.

Microsoft also distinguishes pending remediation actions awaiting approval from completed actions in the Action center. Approval initiates the action; it is not the same as verifying its outcome.

Ask how the file arrived

A path under Downloads is a starting clue. It does not establish the download source or explain every step that put the file there.

Review browser download records where available, relevant mail or web filtering events, deployment records, and user-provided context. Correlate timestamps and file identifiers across those sources. A filename match by itself is too weak to establish the delivery route.

If the evidence points to email, check whether other recipients received the same attachment or link. If it points to a browser, establish whether the source and download were expected. If a deployment tool delivered the file, identify the package, publisher, and approval record.

I would document missing history, inaccessible profiles, and unavailable precursor events explicitly. “Source not established from the records available” is a useful finding. It leaves a clear question for follow-up without turning a plausible story into a fact.

Determine whether it executed

The next question is whether the file was only present or whether there is evidence that it ran. Look for process creation, initiating processes, child processes, file writes, persistence changes, and related network activity in the relevant window.

In Defender, DeviceProcessEvents provides process creation and related events, including initiating-process information. That is one evidence source. A download record answers a different question, and neither source should silently stand in for the other.

Before relying on an empty result, check that the device was reporting, the necessary data was collected, and the event window is still available in the source you searched. Microsoft’s advanced hunting documentation describes its own data availability and retention boundaries. Do not assume every view or connected log store covers the same period.

Keep the conclusion within the evidence

“No execution evidence found in the sources and time window reviewed” is a bounded finding. “The file never executed” is a stronger claim. Record the sources, window, and visibility gaps so the next analyst can tell which conclusion the evidence supports.

Confirmed execution, suspicious follow-on activity, or a significant visibility gap can change the response. I would use the organization’s escalation criteria to decide whether more containment or investigation is needed. A successful file action does not settle those decisions by itself.

Check scope beyond the alerted device

Search the known hash or another confirmed indicator across the environment you are authorized to investigate. Filenames can change, and identical filenames can refer to unrelated files, so treat name-only matches as leads to validate.

Defender’s file investigation view brings together related alerts, observed names, and devices where the file was seen. Its organizational prevalence is limited by access permissions. “No other matches in my search” is therefore different from “no other devices were affected.”

Record which tenant, device groups, sources, and time range the search covered. In an MSP, the boundaries of one customer investigation should remain clear. Check recurring alerts, additional profiles, and connected account activity when the evidence reasonably implicates them.

If broader compromise is plausible, follow the established incident-response path. NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 integrates incident response with cybersecurity risk management, including detection, response, and recovery. The practical lesson here is to connect the alert to the organization’s response process and decision owners.

Make restoration an explicit decision

A user needing a file back is a business requirement to investigate. It is not evidence that the file is safe.

Verify provenance, expected publisher, business purpose, and the reason for the detection before deciding whether restoration is appropriate. Microsoft’s quarantine restoration guidance starts from determining that the quarantined file is not a threat. The presence of a Restore control does not establish that conclusion.

Restoring an item and changing future protection deserve separate decisions. Microsoft recommends defining antivirus exclusions sparingly and reviewing them regularly. If an exception is justified, document its scope, owner, reason, and review point. Avoid using a broad folder or process exclusion as a shortcut around an unresolved detection.

For confirmed malicious content, keep it contained and verify that related artifacts or persistence identified during the investigation were addressed. For a benign file, record the evidence supporting that finding and the approved restoration or exception decision.

Six questions before closing the ticket

This is the checklist I would put in the ticket closeout process. Each answer should connect a conclusion to evidence, a documented limit, or an assigned follow-up.

  1. What was detected? Record the object, detection, device, event time, and original alert reference.
  2. What happened to it? Confirm the actual response outcome, including anything pending or unsuccessful.
  3. Where did it come from? State the best-supported source, or identify what remains unknown.
  4. Did it run? Describe execution evidence, the sources and window searched, and visibility limits.
  5. Was anything else affected? Describe the scope searched and relevant findings without claiming coverage the investigation did not have.
  6. What remains? Record the disposition, restoration decision, user guidance, follow-up owner, or escalation reference.
A closeout structure to copy into your ticket

Use these prompts as a starting point. Replace each placeholder with the actual finding; this is not a completed incident record.

  • Detection: [Object and detection, affected device, event time and time zone, alert reference.]
  • Response: [Action, verified result, verification time, unresolved errors or pending work.]
  • Source: [Evidence supporting the delivery route, or explicit unknown.]
  • Execution: [Findings, sources checked, time window, and collection or retention limits.]
  • Scope: [Tenant and device groups, indicators searched, related findings, inaccessible sources.]
  • Disposition: [Why this can close or must escalate, any approved restoration, and follow-up owner.]

An unanswered question does not automatically require an unlimited investigation. It does require a decision about its significance. If a gap prevents a defensible disposition, keep the work open or hand it to a named escalation owner rather than burying it in the closeout note.

Leave an evidence trail the next analyst can use

The goal is not to turn every blocked download into a multi-hour incident. It is to make the depth of the response match the evidence and risk. A bounded investigation may support closure; an unexpected process or unresolved containment failure may require a broader response.

Put the six questions into your next suspicious-file ticket. When the same alert returns, or another analyst reviews the decision, the record should explain what was checked, what was contained, and why the chosen next step made sense. “Quarantined successfully” can be part of that record. It should not have to carry the whole story.

items.title: Ending The Defender’s Dispatch
items.content_html:
I’m ending The Defender’s Dispatch after 13 issues. Issue 013, published November 9, was the last one.

I started the newsletter to give practical cybersecurity and IT stories more room than a roundup allows. I’m glad I made it, but preparing the web edition and email every week became a source of stress. Some issues went out later than planned, and I don’t want to keep promising a schedule that’s wearing on me.

I wrote a longer note about the decision on the Dispatch page. The full archive will stay online. I’ll keep writing here, including Security Signal Weekly. Thank you to everyone who read, subscribed, or sent a story.

items.title: SonicWall's SAML VPN Bypass: The Questions MSPs Need to Answer
items.content_html:
A ticket that says “SonicWall patched” leaves out the question at the center of CVE-2026-19868: which sign-in routes would the SSL VPN accept, and did they all enforce the intended controls? For an MSP with several client firewalls, that question needs an answer for each deployment, not just a firmware job marked complete.

SonicWall published its SonicOS advisory on November 6. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security says SonicWall has observed exploitation, and CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. That calls for an expedited review. It does not establish that every SonicWall firewall, or every client using one, has been compromised.

The credential condition matters

The published CVE description says a person with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method may be able to bypass SAML authentication controls in the SonicOS SSL VPN service. If MFA is enforced through that SAML route, successful exploitation may bypass that MFA requirement too. The flaw affects the Gen7 and Gen8 SonicOS branches identified in the vendor’s advisory.

Those details set the boundary of the claim. The public description does not say an attacker can connect without any valid credentials. It does show why a configuration labeled “SAML with MFA” is insufficient evidence of protection when another login method is available. The firewall’s actual authentication paths determine what a user can do.

Find the configurations, not just the appliances

Start with the firewalls you manage, then narrow the list by what is reachable and how SSL VPN is configured. For each device, record its model, running SonicOS version, SSL VPN exposure, SAML provider, other enabled login methods, and the owner of the change. A firewall in inventory and an exposed SAML VPN with an alternate credential path are different findings.

Check the current SonicWall advisory against each model and release branch before assigning a fixed build. The Canadian bulletin identifies affected release ranges as of November 6, but the vendor’s current matrix should control the upgrade decision. Record the version you observed on the device and the advisory revision you used. A copied version number with no appliance or branch attached is hard to audit later.

If you establish that an appliance does not use the affected authentication path, record the configuration evidence. If you cannot tell which methods are enabled, leave that client open for investigation. An unverified configuration is not a clean result.

Patch and test the route people actually use

Plan the update as a remote-access change. Back up the configuration through the client’s normal process, agree on a recovery route, and account for the VPN interruption. Avoid leaving an alternate login method enabled for convenience during maintenance without checking what controls it enforces.

After the upgrade, confirm the running firmware version on the appliance. Then use an authorized test account to complete a normal VPN sign-in through the intended SAML provider and MFA flow. Review the sign-in result in both the VPN and identity-provider records. Check the other configured authentication methods against the client’s access policy so a fallback route does not quietly weaken the requirement you just tested.

This is configuration testing during an approved change window, not a reason to run an exploit against a production client firewall. Where you cannot safely test a path, document the limitation and the follow-up owner.

Decide whether the exposed period needs investigation

An update does not explain prior access or invalidate a session that was already established. Preserve available VPN logs and identity-provider sign-in records before retention or routine cleanup removes them. Look for unexpected successful logins, unfamiliar source addresses, access through a method that should not have been allowed, new VPN users, and changes to remote-access or administrative settings.

Treat an unusual event as a lead. Compare it with maintenance windows, expected travel, account activity, and endpoint or network evidence before calling it malicious. If the evidence points to unauthorized access, follow the client’s incident-response process to scope accounts, sessions, and reachable systems. The public advisories confirm exploitation of the vulnerability; they do not attribute a particular client’s log entry to this CVE.

What I would want in the MSP ticket

For each client, the record should answer which appliance and SSL VPN configuration were checked, whether the affected path was present, which firmware was running before and after the change, how the SAML and alternate login routes were tested, what logs were reviewed, and what remains unresolved. Include the vendor advisory and the person responsible for the next step. Keep client identifiers and raw sign-in details out of the public write-up.

Across clients, a small status matrix makes gaps visible: inspected, potentially affected, updated, tested, and still under investigation. That is more useful than a single note saying all SonicWalls were checked. It also gives the next technician a way to distinguish a completed patch from a verified access path.

items.title: Showcase Review: A Movie Night Companion for the iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
One of the things I like about the iPhone Duo is that developers have a reason to think about what a phone can become in your hands. Open it, close it, prop it beside you, and there is an opportunity to give the software a different role. Showcase makes sense to me in exactly that context: a movie and TV tracker that can become a small companion to movie night.

There is some of that early iPhone spirit here: software that gives me a reason to enjoy the device as well as use it. Showcase has a practical job, and I appreciate the willingness to make the hardware part of the experience.

I also bring some history to this category. When I wrote about why Trakt is still my home base for movies and TV, years of watched episodes and ratings were central to the argument. Showcase needs to respect that record while giving me a new reason to enjoy using it.

Disclosure and scope

I received a review code. This review focuses on the iPhone Duo design, with my own device photos and researched feature, pricing, and privacy details. Performance and sync behavior have not been independently verified.

My take

Showcase’s appeal is that keeping track can be part of enjoying movies and television. The visual presentation has somewhere useful to go on the Duo, especially when the phone is sitting beside the couch. It gives the extra screens a role in the activity instead of treating them as spare space.

For someone with an established Trakt account, continuity remains the deciding practical issue. I am interested in Showcase as a more enjoyable daily interface. Before entrusting it with the whole archive, I still want to understand how its connection handles the records I already have.

A place for the Duo beside the couch

Showcase’s version 1.5.2 release notes describe an Up Next presentation on the outer screen when the Duo is in tent or kickstand mode. The queue becomes a sequence of cards that can sit beside you while you catch up.

That is an appealing answer to a real design question: what should the app do when I stop holding the phone like a conventional handset? A nearby display of what comes next suits this job. I can imagine the phone having a place in the evening, rather than being something I pick up, consult, and immediately put away.

It also gives the poster-led presentation a purpose. A watchlist is partly a practical record and partly anticipation. Seeing the next film or episode as a distinct card plays into that second part. The app can feel like a little piece of the entertainment setup.

The test for this kind of design is whether the useful action stays close. An attractive card should still make it clear what I am looking at and how to keep my place. That is where I want the playfulness to lead: an interface I enjoy opening that also makes the next decision easier.

The photos at the top show the Available queue in wide and compact layouts. The wide view fits two columns of cards; the compact view stacks them in one column.

The watchlist has a job to do

The developer’s site describes movie, season, and episode tracking alongside ratings, release alerts, discovery, and friend activity. It also lists widgets, an Apple Watch app, and the ability to snooze a title. Those features fit together around a sensible task: finding the next thing worth watching and remembering where I stopped.

Streaming availability and filters for the services I actually use make that task more practical. Siri support also offers a quick way to ask what is available tonight. I am more interested in those routes to a decision than in a longer list of titles to browse.

Snoozing is a particularly good idea. Following a show should not mean committing to think about it every week. A useful queue needs a way to acknowledge that I am interested but not ready to catch up. The same applies to alerts. A premiere reminder can help; a constant stream of entertainment notifications can become another reason to silence an app.

I would judge discovery by whether it shortens the decision. More recommendations are not automatically more useful. Recommendations from people whose taste I understand have a clearer purpose than another endless selection to browse.

Trakt support is the important part for me

Showcase advertises Trakt sync and imports from Trakt, Letterboxd, and TV Time. That gives existing users a route in. It does not, on its own, establish which fields move in each direction or what happens when two devices disagree.

I would check a small, recognizable part of my history first: an unfinished season, a rewatch, a rating, and a title I removed from my watchlist. Those are different kinds of records. Seeing the right film in a library is only the beginning of confirming that a migration preserved what mattered.

That is a practical reservation, not a finding that Showcase loses data. I have not established that. My preference is simply to keep the existing record until I know how the new app handles it. A tracker becomes much harder to replace after it holds several years of decisions.

The everyday tracking still has to work

The same release notes describe watched and followed changes that persist offline and synchronize when connectivity returns. Release countdowns now use the same local-midnight timing across the app, widgets, and Watch, and notification links open the relevant title directly. These are modest changes individually, but a tracker feels more dependable when its different surfaces agree. Showcase requires iOS or iPadOS 26.

Offline tracking also belongs in the essentials column. Recording an episode on a flight should be an ordinary action. These release notes identify improvements worth checking; they do not substitute for observing those actions on my own devices.

Pricing and privacy

Showcase is free to download, with Showcase Plus costing $1.99 a month, $9.99 a year, or $29.99 for lifetime access. Family Sharing is included for up to five family members. I would establish which features I need and where the free limits appear before choosing a plan. A lifetime option is welcome, but it only becomes good value if the app remains useful.

The privacy question I care about most is who can see my watch history. Before using the friend features or connecting another tracking service, I would check what I am sharing. Showcase’s privacy policy is there for anyone who wants the details.

Who Showcase makes sense for

Showcase belongs on the shortlist for someone who wants movies and TV together, cares about upcoming releases, and enjoys a library with some personality. On the Duo, that personality has a physical context: the phone can sit beside the couch and become part of the experience.

For an established Trakt user like me, the deciding factor is how comfortably it fits around the history already there. If that connection holds up, Showcase offers something I want more of in iPhone software: a useful tool with enough character that opening it is part of the pleasure.

items.title: Security Signal Weekly: October 31-November 6, 2026
items.content_html:
Overview

Several of this week’s most important incidents started in systems that administrators are expected to trust: a security product’s update channel, a WordPress core upgrade, a managed switch, a NAS application, and a hosting provider’s file manager. The cPGuard compromise is the sharpest example. A legitimate updater delivered code that collected root-level credentials and SSH material from thousands of servers, turning a defensive tool into a collection mechanism.

The response cannot stop at installing the newest build. WordPress and Zyxel exploitation, QNAP’s Plex2Shell reports, and the DreamHost breach all require teams to examine the exposed period and invalidate what attackers may already have taken. The same principle applies away from ordinary IT: refrigeration controllers changed physical conditions at blood-storage facilities, while patched mobile flaws were still useful against people who had not updated their phones.

Reality check: An update can close the entry point without removing persistence, restoring a stolen secret, or explaining what happened before the fix. Patch the system, then investigate the window when it was exposed.

Top 10 Security Signals

1. cPGuard’s trusted update channel delivered a credential-stealing backdoor

What happened: OpsShield says an attacker used compromised credentials to access its cPGuard update distribution infrastructure on November 2 and pushed a malicious script through versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19. The vendor advisory says the script collected sensitive server data, while BleepingComputer’s reporting says OpsShield counted 2,946 affected servers and 32 files copied from each one. The targeted material included Linux password hashes, database configuration, root shell history, SSH authorization data, and known hosts.

Why it matters: cPGuard runs on Linux web servers alongside hosting panels and is expected to help protect them. A malicious update therefore arrived through an allowed path with access to credentials that can reach databases, cloud services, other servers, and customer workloads. Installing the clean version removes the known backdoor files but cannot revoke secrets that left the machine.

Action:

  • Identify every server that ran cPGuard 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 and update it to 5.88.25 or later using the vendor’s incident guidance.
  • Rotate root and administrative passwords, database credentials, cloud secrets, and SSH keys that were present on an affected host; remove unrecognized authorized keys and review trust relationships to other systems.
  • Preserve update, shell, authentication, and network logs before cleanup, then investigate the affected server and any systems reachable with the exposed credentials instead of treating the updater fix as incident closure.

2. CISA confirms exploitation of a WordPress core upgrade flaw

What happened: WordPress 7.1.4 fixed CVE-2026-119977, a race condition in the full-package upgrade process that can expose a predictable staging path and allow remote code execution during the upgrade window. The WordPress security release urged immediate updates, and CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 3 after confirming exploitation. Wordfence subsequently reported blocking thousands of attempts, according to current reporting.

Why it matters: This is a WordPress core issue rather than a vulnerable third-party plugin, so the exposure reaches sites that may otherwise have a disciplined extension inventory. The attack condition is tied to an upgrade, which also means a completed update is not proof that the staging path was never abused while the old process was running.

Action:

  • Move every WordPress site to 7.1.4 or a later security release and verify the running core version from the site and management tooling.
  • Review web-server, PHP, file-integrity, and administrative logs around recent core upgrades for unexpected requests, new PHP files, unfamiliar administrators, scheduled tasks, or modified plugins and themes.
  • Keep management access restricted, preserve known-good backups outside the web root, and rebuild or restore a site when evidence shows code execution rather than deleting only the first suspicious file.

3. The earlier Zyxel switch patch did not stop the exploit attackers were using

What happened: Zyxel disclosed CVE-2026-107441, a pre-authentication out-of-bounds write in the GS1900 web management interface that can lead to operating-system command execution. The Zyxel advisory covers ten models. Binarly’s analysis found that the exploit remained effective on firmware previously updated for CVE-2026-7273, and researchers linked the activity to a campaign that compromised 996 switches and collected configurations and credential material.

Why it matters: A switch configuration can reveal VLANs, management paths, SNMP details, and credentials that help an attacker map or re-enter a network. The failed assumption around the earlier patch is also operationally important: a ticket showing that CVE-2026-7273 was remediated did not mean the attack path was closed.

Action:

  • Match every GS1900 switch against Zyxel’s affected-model table and install the latest fixed firmware listed for CVE-2026-107441, even if the June update was already deployed.
  • Move the web interface to an isolated management network, block internet and ordinary user-subnet access, and limit administrative sources to named hosts.
